• EPS NT$11.01, a 17-year high, core business profitability improving

• 2025 outlook is for strong growth; 1Q25 AI server revenue to more than double

• Seeing sustained demand for AI infrastructure and strong capex of major CSPs

• To complete contract signing in 1-2 months for collaboration with Japan automaker

---





14 March 2025, Taipei, Taiwan – Hon Hai Technology Group (“Foxconn”) (TWSE:2317) today announced its full year and fourth quarter 2024 financial results.





Full year 2024 net profit reached NT$152.7 billion, resulting in an earnings per share of NT$11.01, a 17-year high. At the same time, the Group announced that it will distribute a cash dividend of NT$5.80 per share, a record level since its listing in 1991. Despite significant changes in global tariff policies, geopolitical risks and monetary policies, the outlook for 2025 is for strong growth. The company also shared key developments around its three major smart platforms, as well as on AI and EV in 2025.





For the full year 2024, revenue totaled NT$6.86 trillion, up 11.3% on-year. Gross profit reached NT$428.9 billion, up 10.6%; operating net profit, at NT$200.6 billion, was up 20.5%; while net profit rose 7.5% to NT$152.7 billion for the same time period. Gross profit margin, operating profit margin and net profit margin stood at 6.25%, 2.92% and 2.23% respectively, compared with 6.30%, 2.70% and 2.31% in the previous year. With profitability of the core business improving significantly, EPS for the year, at NT$11.01, was up by NT$0.76 on-year.





In the October-December quarter, revenue reached NT$2.13 trillion, rising 15% on-year; gross profit reached NT$131 billion, up 15.7% from the same three months a year ago; operating net profit was NT$64.5 billion, showing an on-year gain of 31.8%; however net profit, at NT$46.3 billion, fell 12.8% for the same time period. Gross profit margin, operating profit margin and net profit margin were 6.15%, 3.03% and 2.17% respectively, compared to 6.12%, 2.64% and 2.87% in the same period a year ago, showing an increase in two of the three margins that indicated an improvement in profitability of the core business. EPS for the final three months of 2024 was NT$3.34, down NT$0.49 from the same period a year ago.





Chairman of Hon Hai Technology Group (Foxconn), Young Liu, said fourth quarter revenue grew strongly both on-quarter and on-year. The record high NT$6.86 trillion in last year’sannual revenue, came as three of four primary product segments – cloud and networking; computing; components and others – all achieved strong growth. The actual performance exceeded expectations.

Based on the Group's goal of an average payout ratio of no less than 40%, Chairman Liu announced a cash dividend of NT$5.80 per share to be distributed for this year, a significant increase from last year's NT$5.40 per share. The payout ratio reached 52.68%, a new high since the company was listed in 1991, and exceeding 50% for the sixth year in a row.





Looking ahead for 2025, Chairman Liu said the full-year operating outlook will be for strong growth, and that first quarter performance will also turn in strong growth compared to the same period last year. The company is now positioned as a technology manufacturing platform service provider. The three major platforms – Smart Manufacturing, Smart EV, Smart City – are the important foundation for developing various technologies and businesses. These platforms are based on key components, modules, systems, software and other fundamental capabilities we have soundly established. In the future, Foxconn will introduce more generative AI to make them even more powerful.





Foxconn will work with global Tier-1 partners to jointly develop and create generative AI solutions or develop large language models in-house to introduce into its three major intelligent platforms. By doing this, it will improve overall operational efficiency, and also enhance competitive advantage. The Group is using AI to produce AI; in Japan we have built a fully automated mobile phone assembly line. This is a good example of our move towards AI.





In the face of market concerns regarding the impact of geopolitics and tariffs on the Group's operations, Chairman Liu said overall ICT industry demand is generally stable this year. In response to changes, we will maintain close contact with our customers and due to our comprehensive global layout make timely adjustments. Through vertical integration, a diversified footprint and close cooperation with customers, the Group will maintain its market leading position.





Chairman Liu predicted that 2025 will be the first year of AI. Global demand is being sustained for AI computing infrastructure, and the capex of major CSPs will maintain strong growth this year. Looking at the first quarter, Foxconn’s AI server revenue is expected to grow more than 100% both quarter-on-quarter and year-to-year. As the GB200 enters mass production, we believe AI server revenue will improve quarter by quarter.

Looking at the full year, AI server revenue will reach the trillion-dollar scale, in local currency terms, accounting for more than half of the Group’s total server share. Foxconn has beenan important co-development partner in new products with major customers, ensuring that we can participate in next generation upon next generation of product development.





The company also believes that the technical methods used by DeepSeek will accelerate the popularization of AI servers for inference, thereby driving an increase in overall computing power demand. For large enterprises and CSPs, high-end AI servers and complete network and storage architectures are still indispensable, so demand for high- end AI servers will continue to grow. In the long run, as the development of edge AI gradually matures, there is likely to be more demand for upgrading personal devices.





AI server training takes a long time. During this period, if there is a failure in the AI server, it will have a great impact on the training time or even the results. Foxconn has always been in a leading position in terms of quality stability. A 40% market share is our most conservative target. We are confident that we can continue to strive for a higher market share.





Regarding collaboration with Japanese automakers, Chairman Liu said he anticipates “contract signing to be completed in one to two months’ time.” During the second half of the year, the MODEL B and the North American variant of the MODEL C are expected to enter mass production, while the manufacturing factory for the electric bus is scheduled to complete certification in the third quarter, expanding shipment capacity.

Chinese researchers have cracked a barrier to the home-grown production of advanced chips by building an extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light source platform that operates at internationally competitive parameters, according to a research paper.

Advertisement

The team, from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, was led by Lin Nan, previously head of light source technology at ASML in the Netherlands.

ASML , the world’s only manufacturer of EUV machines – which are critical for producing chips with nodes below seven nanometres – has been prohibited from selling its most advanced models to China since 2019, thanks to pressure from the US.

In a call to investors on April 16, ASML chief executive Christophe Fouquet said that it was “always possible to generate some EUV light, but it would take many, many years for China to make an EUV machine”.

NVIDIA’s announcement of a $5.5 billion charge in Q1 2026 financial results marks one of the most significant single-quarter financial hits in the company’s history. The write-down stems directly from U.S. export restrictions on its H20 AI chips, which now require licenses to ship to China, Hong Kong, Macau, and other designated countries. This move, finalized in April 2025, forced NVIDIA to reassess its inventory, purchase commitments, and reserves tied to the H20—a chip designed to comply with earlier U.S. export rules but now caught in an escalating geopolitical battle.

Geopolitical Chess: U.S.-China Tensions and the AI Arms Race

The H20 chip, while stripped of some capabilities to meet prior export thresholds, remains a critical component for China’s AI infrastructure. Chinese tech giants like Tencent, Alibaba, and ByteDance had pre-ordered $16 billion worth of H20 chips to power AI models such as DeepSeek’s R1. The sudden licensing requirement undermines those plans, leaving NVIDIA scrambling to pivot.

The U.S. government’s rationale—preventing advanced chips from aiding China’s military or supercomputing efforts—has drawn criticism from NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, who argues that nearly half of global AI researchers are Chinese, many working in U.S. labs. Politically, the Trump administration’s delayed crackdown on H20 exports after NVIDIA pledged a $500 billion U.S. AI infrastructure investment with TSMC highlights the interplay between corporate lobbying and policy. China represents NVIDIA’s fourth-largest market, trailing only the U.S., Singapore, and Taiwan. About Brand Finance

Brand Finance is the world’s leading brand valuation consultancy. Bridging the gap between marketing and finance, Brand Finance evaluates the strength of brands and quantifies their financial value to help organisations make strategic decisions.

Headquartered in London, Brand Finance operates in over 25 countries. Every year, Brand Finance conducts more than 6,000 brand valuations, supported by original market research, and publishes over 100 reports which rank brands across all sectors and countries.

Brand Finance also operates the Global Brand Equity Monitor, conducting original market research annually on 6,000 brands, surveying more than 175,000 respondents across 41 countries and 31 industry sectors. By combining perceptual data from the Global Brand Equity Monitor with data from its valuation database — the largest brand value database in the world — Brand Finance equips ambitious brand leaders with the data, analytics, and the strategic guidance they need to enhance brand and business value.

In addition to calculating brand value, Brand Finance also determines the relative strength of brands through a balanced scorecard of metrics evaluating marketing investment, stakeholder equity, and business performance, compliant with ISO 20671.

Brand Finance is a regulated accountancy firm and a committed leader in the standardisation of the brand valuation industry. Brand Finance was the first to be certified by independent auditors as compliant with both ISO 10668 and ISO 20671 and has received the official endorsement of the Marketing Accountability Standards Board (MASB) in the United States.

Definition of Brand

Brand is defined as a marketing-related intangible asset including, but not limited to, names, terms, signs, symbols, logos, and designs, intended to identify goods, services, or entities, creating distinctive images and associations in the minds of stakeholders, thereby generating economic benefits.

Brand Strength

Brand strength is the efficacy of a brand’s performance on intangible measures relative to its competitors. Brand Finance evaluates brand strength in a process compliant with ISO 20671, looking at Marketing Investment, Stakeholder Equity, and the impact of those on Business Performance. The data used is derived from Brand Finance’s proprietary market research programme and from publicly available sources.

Each brand is assigned a Brand Strength Index (BSI) score out of 100, which feeds into the brand value calculation. Based on the score, each brand is assigned a corresponding Brand Rating up to AAA+ in a format similar to a credit rating.

Brand Valuation Approach

Brand Finance calculates the values of brands in its rankings using the Royalty Relief approach – a brand valuation method compliant with the industry standards set in ISO 10668. It involves estimating the likely future revenues that are attributable to a brand by calculating a royalty rate that would be charged for its use, to arrive at a ‘brand value’ understood as a net economic benefit that a brand owner would achieve by licensing the brand in the open market.

The steps in this process are as follows:

1 Calculate brand strength using a balanced scorecard of metrics assessing Marketing Investment, Stakeholder Equity, and Business Performance. Brand strength is expressed as a Brand Strength Index (BSI) score on a scale of 0 to 100.

2 Determine royalty range for each industry, reflecting the importance of brand to purchasing decisions. In luxury, the maximum percentage is high, while in extractive industry, where goods are often commoditised, it is lower. This is done by reviewing comparable licensing agreements sourced from Brand Finance’s extensive database.

3 Calculate royalty rate. The BSI score is applied to the royalty range to arrive at a royalty rate. For example, if the royalty range in a sector is 0-5% and a brand has a BSI score of 80 out of 100, then an appropriate royalty rate for the use of this brand in the given sector will be 4%.

4 Determine brand-specific revenues by estimating a proportion of parent company revenues attributable to a brand.

5 Determine forecast revenues using a function of historic revenues, equity analyst forecasts, and economic growth rates.

6 Apply the royalty rate to the forecast revenues to derive brand revenues.

7 Discount post-tax brand revenues to a net present value which equals the brand value.

The recent decline in NVIDIA’s stock price—plunging over 30% from its early 2025 peak—has sparked investor anxiety. While the company’s financial results remain robust, with record quarterly revenue of $39.3 billion and 78% year-over-year growth, the sell-off underscores a deeper concern: the escalating U.S.-China trade war and its impact on tech’s global supply chains.

The Immediate Catalyst: Export Restrictions and Trade Tensions

The primary trigger for NVIDIA’s stock decline is the U.S. government’s curbs on shipments of its H20 AI chips to China, which the Biden administration labeled a national security risk. These restrictions, finalized in late 2024, slashed NVIDIA’s potential revenue by an estimated $5.5 billion, sparking a 7% single-day drop in January. The move reflects a broader U.S. strategy to slow China’s AI advancements, but it has also raised concerns about the long-term viability of NVIDIA’s dominant position in the global AI infrastructure market.

The trade war’s escalation is now a two-way street. China has retaliated with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. imports, while also restricting exports of rare earth minerals—critical for semiconductor production. These non-tariff measures threaten to disrupt global supply chains, with the U.S. semiconductor industry already warning of potential shortages.

Beneath the Surface: Strengths and Vulnerabilities

Despite the headwinds, NVIDIA’s financial performance remains a testament to its leadership in AI. Its Data Center segment, which accounts for 90% of revenue, grew 93% year-over-year in Q4 FY2025, driven by partnerships with cloud giants like AWS and Microsoft Azure. The $500 billion Stargate Project—a collaboration with U.S. cloud providers to build AI supercomputers—highlights the scale of demand for NVIDIA’s AI infrastructure.

However, the company’s reliance on China—a key market for its gaming and data center products—is a vulnerability. While gaming revenue fell 22% sequentially in Q4 due to market saturation, the segment’s full-year growth of 9% suggests underlying resilience. Yet, the export restrictions and broader trade tensions could amplify these pressures.

The Geopolitical Elephant in the Room

The U.S.-China tech rivalry is now a full-blown strategic contest. The U.S. is pushing allies to diversify supply chains away from China, while Beijing is accelerating its indigenous innovation agenda. Chinese AI startups like DeepSeek have begun offering low-cost alternatives to NVIDIA’s GPUs, eroding its pricing power.

Meanwhile, the trade war’s ripple effects are hitting global markets. Gold prices hit record highs of $3,389/ounce in April 2025 as investors flee equities, and the euro surged past 1.50 against the dollar. For nvidia, the risks extend beyond China: the U.S. Treasury’s proposed tariffs on Chinese-built vessels and its pressure on third-party nations to curb trade with Beijing could further disrupt demand.

Valuation: Overpriced or Underappreciated?

NVIDIA’s valuation metrics are polarizing. Its trailing P/E of 35.5x is high relative to peers, but its PEG ratio of 1.02—one of the lowest among the “Magnificent Seven” tech giants—suggests investors are pricing in strong growth. Analysts project ~23% annual earnings growth over five years, fueled by AI adoption in healthcare, robotics, and autonomous driving.

Yet, the near-term risks are undeniable. The $5.5 billion revenue hit from China restrictions and the potential for further geopolitical shocks could prolong volatility. Bulls counter that NVIDIA’s $130.5 billion annual revenue (up 114% year-over-year) and $3.6 billion in operating cash flow provide a sturdy foundation.

Conclusion: A Tale of Two Horizons

Investors must weigh short-term headwinds against NVIDIA’s long-term dominance in AI infrastructure. The company’s Blackwell supercomputers, partnerships with cloud titans, and advancements in generative AI and robotics position it to capitalize on a $10 trillion AI market opportunity by 2030.

However, the U.S.-China tech war’s trajectory is the critical wildcard. If tensions ease—and if NVIDIA can navigate export restrictions and competitor pressures—the stock could rebound. But if the conflict deepens, the company’s valuation and growth narrative face significant challenges.

For now, the data suggests cautious optimism: NVIDIA’s 71% non-GAAP gross margins and its $115.2 billion full-year Data Center revenue reaffirm its structural strengths. Yet, investors should remain mindful that geopolitical risks are now central to the tech sector’s valuation. As the saying goes, “In geopolitics, the only certainty is uncertainty”—and NVIDIA’s stock price reflects that reality.

In this high-stakes game, NVIDIA’s fate hinges not just on its technology, but on its ability to navigate a world where trade wars are fought with semiconductors as much as tariffs.

How can a company from an emerging economy manage to make waves in global business?

Ask Embraer. The Brazilian firm also known as Empresa Brasileira de Aeronautica S.A. is the fourth largest commercial aircraft manufacturer in the world, behind Boeing, Airbus and Bombardier. In mid-August, it posted a 54 percent jump in sales and a 35 percent gain in second-quarter earnings.

A new HBS case study on Embraer, presented in Buenos Aires (in a modified version of how such a case might be taught in a standard classroom setting), offered plenty of room for lively debate among conference participants. Questions they considered: What key elements of strategy and competitiveness will help a firm from an emerging market suceed internationally? How can a government assist a company without smothering it?

Another point of central interest in the Embraer example was an ongoing dispute between Embraer and the Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, which has yet to be settled by the World Trade Organization. Conference participants offered a variety of predictions on how they thought the dispute could and should pan out.

According to Professor Pankaj Ghemawat, who led the discussion (while injecting what he called "procedural asides" to demonstrate how the case might be taught in a classroom), the Embraer case also illuminated ways that companies might craft a strategy to balance two spheres of influence: market and non-market forces.

Issues Unique To The Region

The case on Embraer, Ghemawat explained to the audience in his introduction, is one of the first "outputs" of the School's new Latin America Research Center (LARC). It was co-written by Ghemawat with LARC executive director Gustavo Herrero and senior researcher Luis Felipe Monteiro. Ghemawat, who originally started the case for his elective course on Globalization and Strategy, said that it also illustrates the first efforts of the LARC advisory committee to address business issues unique to the region.

"We started talking about what was distinctive about the Latin American context," Ghemawat said of their early meetings, "and about what research and course development efforts in this area—whether by Harvard or by other institutions—really needed to reflect."

The basic macro environment in emerging economies, he explained, is very different from that of developed economies that sometimes end up getting treated as a "base case."

"We talked about the role of government. And, while it's useful to focus on market strategy, the non-market components of strategy were things that needed to be highlighted as well."

Keys For Strategy

"There's a lot going on in the case," Ghemawat warned the audience as the discussion began. "There's a lose-to-a-billion dollar commitment that Embraer is close to making for a new family of aircraft. There's an extraordinarily complex and bitter dispute at the WTO between the Canadian and Brazilian governments about Embraer versus Bombardier in the regional jet market. In addition, Embraer is selling or has sold a fraction of its equity to a French consortium. Plus, an IPO is being planned."

"What problems confront a company that's trying to become internationally competitive? What sorts of problems are Embraer's partnerships trying to overcome?"

As a company, conference participants said, Embraer had made a number of smart moves. Its human resources strategy was rejuvenated for flexibility, so people were motivated to work there. The company had lowered the cost of capital by sharing risks, first with the government and then, through outsourcing, with suppliers. It focused very early on foreign markets, rather than just on the domestic market.

While the company had clearly benefited from its relationship with the government, said one participant, it had somehow avoided being trapped in the government's embrace.

As Ghemawat told the group, "In some sense the Embraer strategy is not very unusual. It's almost a prototypical strategy from one of these environments trying to become internationally competitive.

"When we looked at India and Argentina and a number of other countries, we see islands of competitiveness, where companies have managed to succeed in decoupling themselves from the most negative elements of the domestic environment while retaining the positive elements, as they attempt to become competitive."

"Embraer is an example of the power of not just assuming that because you are based in a country, you necessarily have to be subject to all the disadvantages imposed by that particular context."

"wrapping Up In The Brazilian Flag"

When Ghemawat turned the discussion to the WTO dispute and asked participants for their reactions, most suggested that companies in emerging economies need to brace themselves for such legal battles on the global stage.

One commentator thought this particular dispute would blow over. "I think there's a lot of saber-rattling going on," he explained. "Canada has a very large number of investments in Brazil. Things will calm down."

Added another: "My impression is that the arguments are very biased in favor of the developed country. Secondly, the developed countries are a lot more professional in hiding their own tricks.

"If we got rid of the biases and put all the tricks on the table, the situation is a lot of more balanced than people tend to believe, at least in the developed countries."

Commented a third, "It looks like the company will need to develop a new set of skills. They have managed to be competitive with their global competitors, but now the arena is moving to the WTO, and that's different competition. They are not competing with similar airplanes, they are competing on who convinces the WTO better; and probably they need to work on their government skills.

"Which government will be more efficient in convincing the WTO? It's striking that Canadians are fighting Brazilians… Embraer has to develop, with their government, a way of defending the company, and [defending] the country's interests, as well."

"The temptation is to wrap up in the Brazilian flag and say, 'The big guys always win.'

"There are skills you need negotiating in that new forum that are absolutely critical," he asserted.

No Delusions

One of the purposes of writing the Embraer case, Ghemawat reminded the group, was to bring business-government relations back to the fore. As business moves forward, he said, it's important to keep in mind that in any industry the scope of strategy vis-à-vis government has expanded beyond traditional musings about "How will we influence the government on domestic regulation?"

"We should start thinking about the potential scope for these kinds of issues in globalization. If this is the positive of globalization—the ability to try and transcend the difficulties of your domestic context in order to improve your competitiveness," Ghemawat said, "then one of the downsides, or at least one of the managerial challenges, is that it's hard to imagine these kinds of disputes ceasing very quickly."

One of the biggest delusions in world business, he added, is that governments will entirely step out of the way. "You still need the government for dealing with other national governments, and for representation before groups such as the WTO.

"And non-market strategy also has to expand beyond just thinking about relationships with the government, to thinking about non-governmental organizations which are very much on the rise as well."

Recent geopolitical events, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, are driving renewed interest from Western governments in Embraer’s C-390 military airlifter.

That is according to Embraer Defense & Security chief executive Jackson Schneider, who says countries in Europe and elsewhere are increasingly interested in replacing decades-old military cargo aircraft.

“Many countries in the world… realise that their logistics systems are very old and need to be replaced,” Schneider recently told reporters. “They need to replace [those systems] as soon as possible.”

He adds that Embraer has recently been engaged in “intense” C-390 sales campaigns, including with countries the airframer had not previously targeted as potential buyers.

Schneider attributes the bump in demand to several factors, including the USA’s 2021 exit from Afghanistan. That event prompted US partners – notably those in Europe – to likewise pull forces from the country. It also prompted a broad exodus of Afghan refugees, Schneider notes.

The effort relied entirely on aircraft, including military lifters and commercial charters.

“The Afghanistan withdrawal of troops and refugees… called attention for European countries… that their logistics systems are not up to date,” says Schneider.

Then came Russia’s February invasion of Ukraine, which further highlighted the need by European countries to update ageing military assets. That event is significantly driving up Western military spending, Schneider adds.

“The world will not be the same after the Russian-and-Ukrainian war,” Schneider says. “It initiated, or reinforced, strong interest” in the C-390.

Schneider also says such factors bode well for additional sales of Embraer’s single-engined Super Tucano – specifically, those examples used for pilot training.

Embraer launched the C-390 in 2009 with an order from the Brazilian air force for the KC-390 variant.

Powered by twin International Aero Engines V2500s, the jet can carry payloads weighing up to 26,000kg (57,320lb) and, when fully loaded, has 1,080nm (2,000km) of range, according to Embraer.

The airframer pitches C-390s as capable of fulfilling a variety of missions, including aerial assault and resupply, medical evacuation, search and rescue, and air-to-air refuelling.

In February, news broke that Brazil’s air force had cut its number of KC-390 orders from 28 to 22, a result of budget constraints. Embraer also holds orders from Portugal for five of the aircraft, and from Hungary for two.

Schneider sees significantly greater demand, noting that the global fleet of medium-weight military airlifters stands at about 1,500 aircraft. Those – many of which are variants of Lockheed Martin’s venerable four-engined C-130 – have an average age of more than 30 years.

“These planes will have to be replaced,” Schneider says.

Ashray Lavsi, principal with Efficio Consulting, reports on the current state of relations between China and Taiwan, and how it might affect the global supply of semiconductors.

Taiwan plays an “extremely critical” role in supplying the world with semiconductors, Lavsi notes. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) provides 90% of advanced-design chips, and 60% of all types of semiconductor products. Its biggest competitors are Samsung and Intel, at a distant second and third, with market shares of 18% and 10%, respectively.

Any interruption, therefore, in the flow of semiconductors from Taiwan could have a “catastrophic” effect on global supply chains. Witness the chips shortage of 2021, which forced the automotive industry to cut back on production by 7 million units, resulting in the loss of billions of dollars of revenue.

The biggest threat at the moment concerns China’s stance on Taiwan, which it claims as part of its territory and could choose to invade the island at any time, choking off semiconductor production.

In addition, notes Lavsi, 50% of all containerships in the world move through the Taiwan Strait, so an interruption of vessel traffic there would seriously impact all trade with China. Short of an invasion by China, a blockage of that critical trade route would have a similar impact. “If anything were to happen,” he says, “with even a minor disruption, the domino effect could be massive.”

The threat has intensified in recent in recent months, with China conducting military exercises in the Taiwan Strait. Such actions have caused the U.S. and Europe to begin seeking ways to reduce their reliance on semiconductors from Taiwan, with both offering billions of dollars to companies willing to build domestic chip-fabrication plants. Those efforts are well underway, but are expected to take years to bear results. In the meantime, the stability of the global high-tech supply chain remains dependent on a highly unstable political state of affairs.

China is taking a different tack.

In a notice last week, a state-backed trade association in China issued guidance that would exempt a significant portion of advanced chips from China’s tariffs on the United States.

The reason, experts said, is that China knows it needs those chips and does not want to let its trade war with the United States get in the way.

The upshot is that many advanced chips that are designed by American companies like Nvidia, Apple, Qualcomm and AMD, but manufactured in Taiwan, will not be subject to Chinese tariffs. American companies might end up with the chips, and then sell them to Chinese companies, but for the purposes of tariffs, China will not consider such chips as originating in the United States.

That is a change from typical trade policy. China will consider the location where the circuits were etched onto tiny pieces of silicon to be the place where a chip is made.

Raw Text: IntroductionIn today's interconnected world, geopolitical risks have become a significant factor influencing the stock market, particularly in industries like semiconductors. As a crucial component of everything from smartphones to automobiles, semiconductors are at the heart of technological advancement. However, their global supply chain is highly susceptible to geopolitical tensions, making it essential for investors to understand these risks and adapt their strategies accordingly.Core Concept ExplanationGeopolitical risk refers to the potential for political actions or events in one country to affect the economies or markets of other nations. In the semiconductor industry, these risks can arise from trade wars, regulatory changes, or regional conflicts. Given the industry's reliance on a global supply chain, any disruption can significantly impact production and distribution, leading to volatility in semiconductor stocks.Application and StrategiesInvestors can apply their understanding of geopolitical risks to make informed decisions in the semiconductor sector. Here are a few strategies:By diversifying their portfolios, investors can mitigate the impact of regional geopolitical risks. This involves investing in semiconductor companies from different countries or those with diverse supply chains.Staying informed about international relations and trade policies can help investors anticipate potential risks. This might include following news about trade agreements, tariffs, or sanctions that could affect the semiconductor supply chain.Some semiconductor companies are better equipped to handle geopolitical disruptions due to their strong financial positions or robust supply chain management. Identifying and investing in such resilient companies can reduce risk exposure.Case Study AnalysisA notable example of geopolitical risk impacting the semiconductor industry is the U.S.-China trade war. In 2018, the U.S. imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, and China responded in kind. This conflict affected companies like intel and qualcomm , which rely on both countries for production and sales. The tariffs led to increased costs, supply chain disruptions, and stock price volatility. Investors who recognized these risks early on and adjusted their strategies could have minimized their losses or even capitalized on the market movements.Risks and ConsiderationsWhile understanding geopolitical risks offers strategic advantages, it also presents challenges. Predicting geopolitical events is inherently uncertain, and investors might misjudge the potential impact on the semiconductor industry. The semiconductor industry experienced a robust rebound in 2024, recovering from a significant slump in 2023. This resurgence, largely fueled by AI-driven demand, sets the stage for continuous growth in 2025. The industry's trajectory will be defined by three transformative trends: electrification, digitization, and the prolific adoption of artificial intelligence (#AI) and Internet of Things (#IoT) technologies.

Key verticals driving the semiconductor industry growth include automotive, industrial, aerospace, defense, and high-performance computing (#HPC). Innovations such as #autonomousvehicles, #electricmobility, #smartgrids, and industrial #IoT are thrusting the emergence of #Industry5.0, which emphasizes the integration of human intelligence and advanced technologies. These advancements are creating a surging need for powerful, efficient, and secure semiconductor solutions, solidifying the industry's critical role in enabling next-generation applications and a more connected, sustainable future.

Market Forecasts

Gartner has predicted that the Global semiconductor revenue would surpass the $700 billion mark in 2025, growing at a rate of 13.8 percent. The industry is expected to grow to $1 trillion by 2030.

IDC predicts that the worldwide demand for artificial intelligence (#AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) will continue to grow by more than 15 percent in 2025. They further foresee a double-digit growth for the entire semiconductor industry in 2025.

It is projected that the electronics component industry will recover by Q1 2025. Excess inventory which was a challenge in 2024 will be dealt with production cuts by suppliers and buyers filling backlogs with existing surplus.

As demand stabilizes, especially driven by AI, high-performance computing, and electric vehicles, production will likely align with more sustainable growth patterns. However, supply chain resilience will remain a priority, as companies work to avoid overproduction and ensure that manufacturing capacity aligns closely with evolving market needs, particularly in AI and data center applications.

Data Center Transformation with AI Accelerators

AI adoption is driving an unprecedented surge in demand for semiconductors, with the transition from predictive to generative AI accelerating the need for AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory (#HBM). Traditional machine learning models, such as YOLO-v5, with weights in the sub-500M range, are being ousted by larger, more complex models like Phi, Gemma, and Mistral-7B, which fall into the 5B–70B weight class. This shift reflects the growing computational intensity of modern AI applications.

The growing demand for AI silicon, particularly in data centers, has ballooned Nvidia's data center business to forecasted revenues exceeding $80 billion for 2025.

Furthermore, the traditional dynamics between CPUs (Central Processing Units) and co-processors like GPUs (Graphic Processing Units) or domain-specific ASICs (Application-specific Integration Circuits) are evolving. CPUs increasingly serve as orchestrators or business logic co-processors for GPUs, coordinating a growing array of specialized accelerators. This shift highlights the critical role of diversified semiconductor architectures in meeting the soaring computational demands of generative AI applications.

AI-fueled Shortages may Occur if Demand Skyrockets

PwC estimates suggest that the market for AI-specific silicon will reach $150 billion by 2028. The explosive growth of AI is fueling the demand for HBM (High Bandwidth Memory), SSDs (Solid State Drive), graphics processing units (GPUs), advanced packaging, and other necessary components. It is expected that in 2025, AI would be infused into a wide range of devices. There will be a demand for customization within specific component sectors. For instance, #Nvidia, #Intel, and #AMD have taken the lead in designing AI-centric processors, such as #GPUs and #CPUs, tailored for tasks like natural language processing, deep learning, and generative outputs. In the years ahead, these components are expected to undergo significant advancements, incorporating neuromorphic designs that emulate human brain-like functions. As AI processing will move to the edge, semiconductors designed for #edge devices will have to be more power-efficient, quicker, and suitable for handling complex AI workloads. This will demand innovation in low-power, high-performance chips, particularly for applications such as #IoT devices, smart cameras and autonomous drones.

The rapid adoption of advanced products like #HBM3 and #HBM3e, essential for AI accelerators, alongside the anticipated launch of next generation #HBM4 in late 2025, is fueling growth in the memory segment. The robust demand for high-end mobile phone #ICs, advanced node ICs for AI servers, and WiFi7 will propel an increase of 13 percent in the non-memory segment. A recovery in the consumer electronics market will create demand for mature node ICs. AI-enabled PCs, smartphones and other devices are contributing to the growth. As per estimates from Canalys AI laptops will account for 50 percent of global PC shipments. IDC had predicted that generative AI smartphone shipments would increase 364 percent year-over-year in 2024, reaching 234.2 million units in 2025, at a growth rate of 73.1 percent. IDC also opined that Global Gen AI smartphone shipments would reach 912 million units, with a CAGR of 78.4percent during the period of 2023 until 2028.

High Demand for Memory Market and Move Towards HBM Customization

Memory and Logic products make up the major share of the semiconductor market. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) and enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs) are experiencing sustained demand driven by the proliferation of AI applications. Gartner forecasts a 57 percent increase in HBM shipments for 2025, building on the remarkable 265 percent growth recorded in 2024. However, this increase in demand has led to supply bottlenecks and shortages. To address this, industry leaders such as Samsung Electronics, Micron Technology, and SK Hynix have adjusted their production capacities to prioritize HBM. As HBM supplies become limited, manufacturers will invest greater capacity and resources into building custom HBMs.

“There is a big wave coming in HBM architectures — custom HBM. The proliferation of AI infrastructure requires extreme efficiency with a scale-out capability, and we are in solid agreement with our key customers that customization of HBM-based AI will be a critical step. PPA — power, performance, and area are the keys for AI solutions, and customization will provide a significant value when it comes to PPA”. - Indong Kim, Vice President and Head of DRAM Product Planning at Samsung Semiconductor.

The #HBM market leaders are working on new ways to increase performance and processing speeds. #Samsung and #Micron are adopting advanced techniques, including the use of a non-conductive film (#NCF) combined with thermocompression bonding (TCB) at each bump level. In contrast, #SKHynix is utilizing a flip-chip mass reflow process with molded underfill (MR-MUF), which encapsulates the stack in a high-conductivity molding material in a single step. These leaders have also navigated rigorous client-specific qualification processes; for instance, Samsung’s HBM3E products recently passed Nvidia’s tests for use in its AI processors. Meanwhile, demand for #DRAM and #NAND flash remains subdued due to inventory surpluses.

Advanced Packaging Techniques

In 2024, as the functionality and performance requirements of semiconductor wafers continue to improve, advanced packaging technologies will become a major focus. Industry leaders like Nvidia are leveraging TSMC’s chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (#CoWoS) technology to improve chip performance by stacking chips on a single substrate, improving performance, reducing footprint, and boosting power efficiency. As node sizes continue to shrink, #CoWoS is emerging as a key solution for advancing semiconductor capabilities, particularly in AI applications. Meanwhile, #FOPLP (Fan-Out Panel-Level Packaging), currently applied for smaller analog chips like #PMIC and #RF, is expected to see robust growth from 2025 onward. With ongoing technological advancements, #FOPLP is anticipated to penetrate the AI chip market, which requires larger packaging areas, and enables more advanced glass base products. In response to rising demand, especially from high-performance computing customers such as #NVIDIA, #AMD, #AWS, #Broadcom, and cloud service providers (#CSPs), #TSMC plans to expand its #CoWoS production capacity. The target is to increase production from 330,000 wafers in 2024 to 660,000 wafers in 2025, marking a 100 percent annual increase, with the CoWoS-L product line growing by 470 percent annually. This surge in production will also create growth opportunities for Taiwan’s equipment supply chain, including key process equipment vendors in areas such as wet etching, dispensing, and crystal picking. #CoWoS and #FOPLP technologies are thus playing critical roles in meeting the growing demand for advanced AI and high-performance computing chips while advancing semiconductor innovation.

A Defining Year (2025) for 2nm Technology

All major wafer makers have entered 2nm mass production. TSMC is rapidly expanding its fabs in Hsinchu and Kaohsiung, which is projected to enter mass production in the second half of 2025. Samsung can possibly enter production sooner than TSMC. #Intel may concentrate on 18A, which already has Backside Power Delivery Network, #BSPDN, under strategic adjustment. These three major wafer makers will encounter roadblocks in balancing performance, power consumption and cost per area with the 2 nm technology. The mass production of key products using this technology, such as Smartphone AP, Mining Chip, AI Accelerator, will also start in 2025.

Automotive Electronics and EV Semiconductors

The automotive sector, particularly with the rise of electric vehicles (#EVs), is experiencing a profound transformation as cars evolve from mechanical systems with wheels to advanced electronic systems. EVs require three times the semiconductor components compared to traditional vehicles, driven by the need for more advanced technologies. Semiconductors play a vital role in enabling reliable and secure communication between vehicles and their environment (#V2X), enhancing the overall driving experience for both passengers and drivers. Sensors embedded in EVs provide real-time understanding of the environment, user behavior, and the vehicle's own performance. Wide-bandgap (#WBG) semiconductors such as silicon carbide (#SiC), gallium nitride (#GaN), and alternative materials such as gallium oxide (#Ga2O3) are revolutionizing the auto semiconductor industry with greater energy efficiency, power density and resistance to higher temperatures. Major power semiconductor suppliers, including #STMicroelectronics, #3Onsemi, #Infineon, #Nexperia and #ROHM are increasingly concentrating on #WBG technology.

Meanwhile, processors facilitate self-learning algorithms that enable real-time decision-making for various functions. The rise of software-defined vehicles demands high-performance computing integrated circuits (#ICs), zonal controllers, and smart peripherals that can be updated and programmed over-the-air (#OTA). Specialized chips are required for powertrain management, battery management systems (#BMS), autonomous driving, and in-vehicle infotainment systems, making automotive-grade semiconductors a critical segment of the market. As this shift accelerates, automotive semiconductors will become an increasingly essential part of the semiconductor industry's growth trajectory.

Robust Demand for Advanced Nodes, 3D chip Architecture and Accelerated Foundry Expansion

Semiconductor manufacturers are redefining the limits of Moore's Law through breakthroughs in 3D chip stacking and advanced nodes below 5nm. These bleeding-edge technologies enhance performance, energy efficiency, and chip density, catering to the growing demands of AI, high-performance computing, and next-generation devices. AI is driving the expansion of advanced nodes (below 20nm). Advanced nodes’ capacity is rising by 12 percent annually while wafer manufacturing in general will increase by 7 percent in 2025. Average capacity utilization rate is expected to be above 90 percent. Global leaders like #TSMC and #Samsung are at the forefront of adopting these advanced manufacturing techniques, driving innovation across the industry. TSMC is building 2nm and 3nm in Taiwan and 4/5nm in the U.S. which will soon be in mass production. Samsung is improving on its 2nm in Hwaseong, Korea, building on its advantage of entering GAA (Gate All Around) generation first. Intel’s focus is on 18A process development.

Meanwhile, Indian research institutions and startups are forging partnerships with international players to develop scalable solutions for these advanced architectures, positioning themselves as key contributors to the global semiconductor ecosystem.

5G Expansion and 6G Evolution

The 5G rollouts and initial developments in 6G are driving semiconductor demand. 5G enables remarkable breakthroughs in healthcare, transportation and entertainment industry, enabling remote surgeries, smart city management, asset tracking, supporting self-driving cars and creating immersive virtual reality experiences. As the demand for 5G grows, miniaturization and integration become crucial in semiconductor design. A major innovation in this field is the development of System-on-Chip (#SoC) designs. These designs combine processors, memory, and radio frequency (#RF) components on a single chip, streamlining functionality and minimizing space needs. By embedding multiple functions into one chip, SoCs help meet the demands of faster, more efficient #5G networks. Advanced semiconductor chips are integral for the enhanced processing capabilities required in 5G base stations. Smartphones and other mobile devices depend on powerful semiconductors to support 5G connectivity. The IoT ecosystem also benefits enormously from 5G technology and supporting semiconductors. Advanced communication infrastructure necessitates semiconductors that enable higher bandwidth, optimized energy efficiency and speed.

Quantum Computing

The United Nations has declared 2025 as the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology. Quantum computing, while still in its developmental phase, is gradually emerging as a transformative technology for industries commanding massive computational power. Behemoths such as IBM, Google, and Intel are making significant advancements in quantum processor development. It is expected that within the next few years quantum chips will scale up significantly.

Rising Demand for Power Components Driven by Data Center Growth and the Subsequent Power Shortages

The data center industry has been subjected to a major roadblock with not enough power or space to support the heightened AI demand and subsequent need to host the enormous data. A CNBC report pointed out that the power demand for the data centers due to the AI boom may match up to the electricity demand for major cities and U.S states. Many power grids around the world are several decades old, nearing the end of their 50–80-year lifecycles. This aging infrastructure makes them increasingly susceptible to power outages, cyber-attacks, and community emergencies. A 21st-century power grid must meet the growing demand for electricity driven by electric vehicles, heat pumps, industrial electrification, and hydrogen electrolysis. Additionally, it needs to expand into new regions to tap into optimal wind and solar resources. These factors highlight the need for a larger grid with enhanced long-distance transmission capabilities. This is leading to new developments in the power component industry. High-efficiency power converters can reduce data centers' energy loss by using new materials that are more efficient than traditional silicon-based components. These include silicon carbide (#SiC) and gallium nitride (#GaN) components, which provide significantly higher breakdown voltage, faster switching speeds, higher power density, and smaller size. #Wolfspeed, #STMicroelectronics, and #Infineon manufacture #SiC and/or #GaN components. #Wolfspeed, a leader in SiC technology, is actively working to expand its global presence and boost production capacity. Similarly, GaN, which was once predominantly used in aerospace and defense, is now finding growing applications in communications and data centers. SiC and #GaN components produce less emissions and can help companies achieve sustainability goals sooner due to power efficiency.

Sustainability and Green Semiconductor Manufacturing

Rising environmental concerns will drive the adoption of sustainable manufacturing practices and will encourage manufacturers to scrutinize emissions throughout the supply chain. Chip fabrication creates colossal amounts of emissions due to manufacturing tools, chemicals, raw materials, and extensive subfab facilities. As a result, chip manufacturers are switching to alternative fuels such as biogas and green hydrogen to facilitate sustainable operations. They are also replacing conventional chemicals with recycled materials. Fabs capture hazardous gases through membrane separation, cryogenic recovery, or desorption and incorporate sustainability in their internal processes.

Supply Chain Disbalances

The semiconductor supply chain is inherently complex and highly sensitive, requiring coordination across multiple stages, specialized processes, and diverse geographic regions. It involves over 5,000 vendors working in tandem, many of which supply a single component to a single company. This intricate interdependence means any disruption can bring the entire industry to a standstill.

Adding to this complexity are geopolitical tensions and demand volatility. The absence of competition in the GPU market, for instance, has concentrated most demand on Nvidia. Bain & Company projects that capital spending on data centers will rise by 36 percent year-over-year in 2024, driven by AI and accelerated computing. If the demand for current-generation GPUs doubles by 2026, suppliers will boost output by 30 percent or more to meet requirements—an ambitious challenge.

A report from Bain & Company further warns of an imminent AI-induced semiconductor shortage. Anne Hoecker, Head of Bain’s Americas Technology Practice, highlights the extraordinary demand for GPUs and other components driven by AI-enabled devices. She notes, “The increasing demand for GPUs has caused shortages in some segments of the semiconductor supply chain. The onslaught of AI-enabled devices may accelerate PC refresh cycles and pose extreme widespread supply constraints for semiconductors.” Bain also emphasized that an increase in demand beyond 20 percent could significantly exacerbate supply chain complexities.

The semiconductor supply chain’s delicacy, combined with its global interconnectedness and growing demand for AI and accelerated computing, underscores the urgency of addressing these looming challenges.

Governments and corporations are increasingly adopting localization strategies to reduce the risks associated with over-reliance on specific regions for semiconductor production. In the United States, the CHIPS Act dedicates $52 billion to strengthening domestic manufacturing and fostering innovation in the semiconductor sector. Similarly, Europe’s Chips Act has allocated €43 billion to establish a more self-reliant and resilient semiconductor ecosystem. These initiatives aim to decentralize global supply chains, enhance regional competitiveness, and safeguard against disruptions in critical industries.

Southeast Asia's Rise as a Semiconductor Manufacturing Hub

Southeast Asia is emerging as a critical player in the global semiconductor supply chain, driven by increasing investments from multinational companies seeking to diversify their manufacturing bases. The U.S.-China trade tensions and lessons from the pandemic have encouraged companies to adopt a "China+1" strategy. Countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, and Thailand are becoming attractive destinations due to their cost competitiveness, proximity to existing supply chains, and business-friendly policies. Governments in Southeast Asia are offering incentives, tax breaks, and infrastructure development to attract semiconductor investments. Samsung and Amkor have set up advanced facilities for chip assembly and testing in Vietnam. Malaysia has seen significant infusion of investments in chip packaging and testing from companies such as Intel and Infineon. Countries like the Philippines and Indonesia are investing in STEM education and workforce development to build a talent pipeline for high-tech manufacturing. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) agreement is expected to further strengthen trade ties and facilitate smoother supply chain integration within the region.

Rise of India as a Semiconductor Powerhouse

In 2024 India introduced the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and saw initial commitments from prominent players such as Vedanta-Foxconn and Micron Technology. The priority was on building foundational infrastructure and fostering industry-academia collaborations. India’s semiconductor roadmap is defined by the ISM which targets to attract $20 billion investments over the next 10 years. The policies are geared at building talent pool in collaboration with the academia, funding for R&D and incentives for setting up fabrication units. India aims to become a preferred destination for global semiconductor manufacturing and design.

Semiconductor Talent Shortage Continues

The semiconductor talent shortage is expected to remain a persistent issue in 2025, impacting companies across the entire supply chain. According to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA), the global semiconductor industry will require over 1.2 million skilled workers by 2030 to meet the growing demand for chips. The World Economic Forum (WEF) projects that by 2025, the global semiconductor industry will face a shortage of over 100,000 engineers, particularly in roles related to chip design, systems integration, and advanced packaging. The Asia Semiconductor Alliance (ASA) estimates that by 2025, 50% of global semiconductor firms in Asia will battle to meet demand for skilled workers, particularly for roles related to R&D and manufacturing. This is aggravated by the shift toward more complex processes such as 3nm and 2nm chip manufacturing that require highly specialized skills. North America and Europe are expected to encounter substantial talent shortages, with 60% of U.S. semiconductor companies indicating that they cannot find enough qualified workers to support their operations. European countries face a similar scenario, with an estimated shortage of 30,000 semiconductor engineers by 2025, according to the European Semiconductor Association (ESA). AI boom and high-performance computing (HPC), heightens demand for professionals skilled in AI chip design, memory architecture, and HPC infrastructure is intensifying.

IDC projects that the demand for semiconductor talent in AI-related fields will grow by 20-30% annually through 2025, placing further strain on the already scarce pool of specialized engineers. The average age of semiconductor workers is rising, with 35-40% of the workforce in many mature markets such as the U.S. and Japan nearing retirement age. The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) predicts that this demographic shift could significantly worsen the talent shortage in the next five years.

Conclusion

The semiconductor industry's recovery in 2024 has set the stage for a transformative 2025, with strong growth driven by AI, IoT, electrification, and the ever-evolving demands of sectors such as automotive, industrial, and high-performance computing. However, as the industry embraces cutting-edge technologies like AI accelerators, high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, and 3D chip architectures, it must maneuver challenges including talent shortages, supply chain complexities, and the need for sustainable practices. As companies increasingly adopt strategies to ensure resilience, localization, and innovation, the semiconductor industry is poised to play a pivotal role in shaping the future of technology, enabling the digital, green, and AI-driven economy of tomorrow.

(Source: KPMG, PwC, IDC, Gartner, Sourceengine, Orbit and Skyline)

ASML Holding N.V. delivered its Q1 2025 financial results on April 16, 2025, revealing a challenging near-term environment for the semiconductor equipment giant. While the company’s total net sales of €7.74 billion and net income of €2.36 billion marked year-over-year declines of 16.4% and 12.3%, respectively, the results underscored strategic investments and long-term growth ambitions in advanced lithography technologies. The performance reflects broader semiconductor industry dynamics, including cyclical demand fluctuations and supply chain uncertainties, yet ASML reaffirmed its vision of becoming a €44–60 billion revenue powerhouse by 2030.

Sales and Income: Navigating a Downward Quarter

Q1 2025 sales fell to €7.74 billion, down from €9.26 billion in Q1 2024 and €9.3 billion in the prior quarter. The drop was driven by fewer system deliveries (73 units vs. 119 in Q1 2024) and weaker demand for installed-base services. Net bookings also slumped to €3.94 billion, a 44.4% YoY decline, signaling cautious customer spending. Despite these headwinds, gross margin held steady at 54.0%, reflecting cost discipline and pricing power, while operating margin declined slightly to 35.4% due to higher R&D investments.

Net income of €2.36 billion, or €6.00 per share, represented a 12.3% YoY drop, primarily tied to lower sales volume. However, management emphasized that the quarter’s performance was consistent with its “expansion years” strategy, prioritizing long-term growth over short-term profits.

Strategic Drivers: AI, EUV, and the $500B Semiconductor Opportunity

ASML’s CEO, Christophe Fouquet, framed the results within the context of the AI revolution, which is driving exponential demand for advanced semiconductors. The company’s EUV and DUV lithography systems remain critical to enabling 3nm and smaller chip geometries, positioning ASML as a key beneficiary of the $500 billion addressable market for AI-driven compute infrastructure.

The Q1 results included €1.2 billion in EUV bookings, underscoring sustained demand for its high-end systems despite macroeconomic volatility. ASML also announced a 4.9% dividend increase to €6.40 per share for 2024, alongside €2.7 billion in Q1 share buybacks, signaling confidence in its balance sheet (€12.7 billion in cash as of Q4 2024).

Outlook: 2025 Guidance and the Road to €60B

Despite Q1’s softness, ASML maintained its full-year 2025 net sales guidance of €30–35 billion, implying a 6–24% YoY growth trajectory from 2024’s €28.3 billion. The wide range reflects uneven AI adoption across customers, with some clients accelerating investments while others delay projects.

Looking further ahead, ASML’s 2030 roadmap targets annual sales of €44–60 billion, driven by:

1. EUV Scaling: High-NA EUV systems enabling 2nm nodes and beyond.

2. DUV Renaissance: Demand for mature-node chips in automotive and industrial sectors.

3. AI Synergy: Collaboration with chipmakers like TSMC and Intel to co-develop next-gen lithography solutions.

Risks and Considerations

The path to €60 billion is not without hurdles. Near-term risks include:

- Demand Volatility: Semiconductor capital expenditure (CapEx) tied to AI adoption remains uneven, with some hyperscalers prioritizing near-term profitability over long-term R&D.

- Supply Chain Constraints: Component shortages and geopolitical tensions could delay EUV shipments.

- Competitive Pressures: Rival Nikon’s advancements in EUV technology, though still years behind ASML’s leadership.

Conclusion: A Cyclical Dip, Not a Structural Shift

While Q1 2025 results reflect the challenges of a maturing semiconductor cycle, ASML’s financial resilience and strategic focus on AI-driven innovation position it to capitalize on the industry’s long-term growth. The company’s gross margin stability, robust cash reserves, and €30–35 billion 2025 guidance suggest that investors should view the current downturn as a cyclical correction rather than a loss of competitive moat.

With AI investment expected to add $1 trillion to global GDP by 2030, ASML’s role in enabling advanced chip manufacturing makes it a critical player in this transformation. As the industry transitions from “Moore’s Law” to “More-than-Moore” innovation, ASML’s technology leadership and customer partnerships will be key to unlocking its €60 billion potential. For investors, the near-term volatility presents an opportunity to buy into a secular growth story at a discounted valuation—provided they can endure the cyclical headwinds ahead.

The semiconductor supply chain is a critical component of the global technology ecosystem, supporting industries ranging from consumer electronics to automotive manufacturing. However, this intricate network faces several threats that can disrupt production and lead to significant economic consequences. Understanding these threats is crucial for stakeholders aiming to build a more resilient semiconductor supply chain.

1. Geopolitical tensions

Geopolitical tensions are a significant threat to the semiconductor supply chain. Trade disputes, export restrictions, and sanctions can hinder the flow of essential materials and technologies. For example, the ongoing trade tensions between the US and China have led to export controls on semiconductor technologies, affecting the operations of companies like Huawei and creating ripple effects throughout the supply chain. Additionally, countries are increasingly imposing regulations to protect their domestic industries, which can disrupt global collaboration and increase production costs.

2. Natural disasters and climate change

Semiconductor manufacturing is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and typhoons can damage fabrication plants (fabs) and interrupt the production process. Climate change exacerbates these risks by increasing the frequency and severity of extreme weather events. For instance, the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan severely affected semiconductor production, causing supply chain disruptions that were felt worldwide. Find out how the supply chain can be more resilient against natural disasters, here.

3. Supply chain bottlenecks

The semiconductor supply chain involves several stages, from raw material sourcing to chip design, fabrication, and testing. Each stage is complex and requires specialised equipment and materials. Any bottleneck in this chain, such as a shortage of silicon wafers or advanced manufacturing equipment, can delay production and lead to supply shortages. The recent global chip shortage highlighted how bottlenecks in the supply chain can have far-reaching impacts on industries like automotive and consumer electronics.

4. Dependence on a limited number of suppliers

A significant threat to the semiconductor supply chain is its dependence on a few key suppliers for critical components and materials. For instance, a small number of companies dominate the market for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and advanced materials like photoresists. This concentration makes the supply chain vulnerable to disruptions if any of these suppliers face production issues, regulatory hurdles, or geopolitical pressures.

5. Technological complexity and innovation cycles

The semiconductor industry is characterised by rapid technological advancements and short innovation cycles. As chips become more advanced, the manufacturing process becomes more complex and requires highly specialised equipment and expertise. This complexity can create vulnerabilities in the supply chain, as even minor errors or equipment failures can lead to significant production delays. Moreover, staying at the forefront of technology requires continuous investment in research and development, which can strain resources and create competitive pressures.

6. Cybersecurity threats

Cybersecurity is an emerging threat to the semiconductor supply chain. As the industry becomes more digitised, the risk of cyber-attacks on manufacturing facilities, design centres, and supply chain management systems increases. A successful cyber-attack can result in intellectual property theft, production disruptions, and compromised product integrity. Ensuring robust cybersecurity measures throughout the supply chain is essential to protect against these threats.

7. Economic and market fluctuations

The semiconductor supply chain is sensitive to economic and market fluctuations. Economic downturns can lead to reduced demand for electronic products, affecting semiconductor production and investment in new technologies. Conversely, sudden surges in demand, such as those driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, can strain the supply chain and lead to shortages. Market dynamics, including competition and price volatility, also influence the stability of the supply chain.

8. Raw material scarcity

Semiconductors require high-purity raw materials like silicon, rare earth elements, and other specialised chemicals. Scarcity or supply disruptions of these materials can significantly impact semiconductor production. Factors such as mining restrictions, geopolitical tensions, and environmental regulations can affect the availability of essential raw materials. For example, the supply of rare earth elements is concentrated in a few countries, making the supply chain vulnerable to geopolitical and market fluctuations.

9. Regulatory and compliance challenges

The semiconductor industry is subject to stringent regulations and compliance requirements, including export controls, environmental standards, and intellectual property protections. Navigating these regulations can be challenging, especially for companies operating across multiple jurisdictions. Non-compliance can result in legal penalties, production halts, and damage to a company’s reputation. The evolving regulatory landscape, driven by concerns over national security, environmental sustainability, and market competition, adds further complexity to the supply chain.

Mitigating the threats

To mitigate these threats, companies and governments are taking steps to enhance the resilience of the semiconductor supply chain. Strategies include diversifying the supplier base, increasing investments in domestic semiconductor manufacturing, and developing more sustainable and secure sourcing practices. Additionally, adopting advanced technologies like artificial intelligence and blockchain can improve supply chain visibility and efficiency, helping to identify and address potential disruptions more effectively.

Conclusion

The semiconductor supply chain faces a multitude of threats that can have wide-ranging impacts on global industries. From geopolitical tensions and natural disasters to technological complexities and cybersecurity risks, these challenges highlight the need for a more resilient and adaptive supply chain. By understanding and addressing these threats, stakeholders can help ensure the continued growth and stability of the semiconductor industry.
